truce

TROOSS -- one syllable, rhymes with 'goose'. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Truce is temporary stop to hostilities.

The two gaming clans agreed to a weekend truce while the tournament servers were being repaired.

Example

After months of shouting matches over the shared driveway, the neighbors shake hands and agree to a truce: at least until the holidays are over, nobody mentions the fence.

A truce is a temporary stop to hostilities. It doesn't settle the quarrel; it just quiets it for an agreed stretch of time.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

respite: A respite is a short break from anything difficult -- illness, work, bad weather -- and it needs no enemy at all. A truce is a pause agreed between opponents in a conflict. A storm can give soldiers a respite, but only the two sides themselves can call a truce.

lull: A lull is a quiet stretch that simply happens -- the fighting, the storm, or the noise dies down on its own for a while. A truce is chosen: both sides agree to stop. A lull can end without warning; a truce is broken, because someone gave their word.

moratorium: A moratorium is an agreed pause on one activity -- a moratorium on new construction, on testing, on fishing -- and it needs no enemies. A truce needs a conflict: it pauses the fighting between opponents. Officials declare a moratorium on an activity; rivals call a truce with each other.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hostilities: acts of open fighting

conflict: a serious ongoing disagreement or struggle

Where it sits · how formal and lasting the pause is — ceasefire → truce → armistice

ceasefire vs. truce: Ceasefire is the battlefield order, truce the broader pact -- a ceasefire stops the shooting at an agreed hour, while a truce can quiet any feud, from trenches to siblings' bedrooms.

armistice vs. truce: Armistice outweighs truce: a truce is a temporary, often informal pause, while an armistice is a formal, signed agreement between nations that can end the fighting for good.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — treow-

root — treow-: faith, pledge, promise (Old English treow)

Put it together

Put it together: Truce comes from Old English treow, 'faith, pledge' -- the same family as true and trust. It began as a plural, 'trewes': pledges exchanged between enemies. Every truce still rests on exactly that -- each side trusting the other's promise to hold fire.

Use the root in a new word: trust

Use the root in a new word: trust: It took years for the two former rivals to rebuild their trust.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Truce lives in conflict: enemies call, declare, or break a truce, and an 'uneasy truce' is one nobody quite trusts. It is always temporary -- lasting peace is a treaty's job. And it needs opponents: friendly coworkers don't have truces, because camaraderie isn't a conflict.
